basic_info.name: HL7 International Patient Summary (IPS) - FHIR Implementation Guide
basic_info.description: The International Patient Summary (IPS) is a global HL7 FHIR Implementation Guide that defines a minimal, non-exhaustive, specialty-agnostic and condition-independent electronic health record extract about a subject of care, intended for unplanned and cross-border care. It is the FHIR realisation of the ISO 27269 dataset (formerly CEN/EN 17269), and its current published edition is v2.0.1 (STU 2, Trial Use, maturity level 3), built on FHIR R4 (4.0.1). The single most load-bearing fact is that the IPS is not free text and not a proprietary note format: it is a Composition-based document Bundle whose first entry is an IPS Composition carrying a fixed set of clinically named, SNOMED/LOINC-coded sections (mandatory Problems, Allergies and Intolerances, and Medication Summary; recommended Immunizations, Diagnostic Results, History of Procedures, Medical Devices; optional Alerts, Advance Directives, Functional Status, History of Past Problems, History of Pregnancy, Patient Story, Plan of Care, Social History, Vital Signs), each populated from standard HL7 IPS profiles such as Condition (IPS), AllergyIntolerance (IPS), MedicationStatement/Request (IPS), Observation Results (IPS) and Vital Signs. Sections are never silently omitted - absent data must be declared through emptyReason or an explicit 'no known X' entry, which is a patient-safety rule the kiosk can adopt directly. IPS is governed by HL7 International (Patient Care work group), was derived from the 2010 EU/US eHealth cooperation (Trillium Bridge, INTERPAS), and is now profiled by jurisdictions worldwide - most importantly for MediKiosk, NRCeS has published an India-localised derivative, the Indian Patient Summary (INPS), in the ABDM FHIR IG v7.0.0 preview, built from IPS v2.0.0. IPS is the canonical prior art for 'a standards-based summary document'.
basic_info.organization: HL7 International, Patient Care work group (primary editors Rob Hausam, John D'Amore, Giorgio Cangioli), in collaboration with CEN TC 251 and ISO (ISO 27269), the Joint Initiative Council, SNOMED International (Global Patient Set / IPS Terminology), IHE (sIPS profile) and the European Commission/HL7 Europe. Contributors include Epic, Accenture, Canada Health Infoway and national programmes.
basic_info.country: International / multi-jurisdiction (originating from EU-US collaboration; implemented across the EU via MyHealth@EU/eHDSI and in Canada, New Zealand, NHS England, Argentina, Netherlands, Cyprus, Japan and others via the G7-IPS roadmap and GDHP).
basic_info.status: Production / published standard in Trial Use (STU 2). Current published edition v2.0.1 (errata release, announced by HL7 on 2026-06-18, generated 2026-06-19). Preceding editions: STU 2.0.0 (final, 2025-10), STU 2.0.0-ballot (2024-08), STU 1.1.0 (2022-11), STU 1.0.0 (2020-05). The IG is balloted as STU with stated intent to become normative in a subsequent ballot cycle. A separate European Patient Summary IG (HL7 Europe, v1.0.0-ballot) is in ballot and conforms to IPS v2.0.0.

technical_features.what_it_does: IPS specifies how to represent a patient summary as a computable FHIR R4 document. It provides (a) the ISO 27269 dataset as a logical model, (b) a Composition profile defining the document's structure, metadata and section list, (c) an IPS Library of resource profiles for the data each section may carry, and (d) generation/consumption guidance (including a $summary operation and a CapabilityStatement). The summary is deliberately minimal: it is the smallest set of clinically relevant facts needed for safe unplanned care, and it explicitly allows sections to be present but empty provided the absence is declared (emptyReason) or stated (e.g., 'no known allergies'). Functionally for MediKiosk Module C it is the reference design pattern: a named-section Composition Bundle where each section is backed by coded, typed resources rather than free prose.
technical_features.architecture: FHIR R4 (4.0.1) Implementation Guide (usable as-is with R4B; packages available for both). Output is a Bundle of type document whose first entry is the IPS Composition, with all other entries referenced from it. The Composition profile (Composition-uv-ips) fixes a section list with slice names, required/optional flags and entry bindings. The IPS Library supplies profiles: Condition (IPS), AllergyIntolerance (IPS), MedicationStatement/Request/Medication (IPS), Immunization (IPS), DiagnosticReport (IPS), Observation Results - Laboratory/Pathology (IPS) and Radiology (IPS), Specimen (IPS), Procedure (IPS), DeviceUseStatement/Device (IPS), Device - Performer/Observer (IPS), ImagingStudy (IPS), Observation pregnancy status/EDD/outcome (IPS), Observation social history tobacco/alcohol (IPS), Flag - Alert (IPS), Patient/Practitioner/PractitionerRole/Organization (IPS), and base Vital Signs. Section slicing rules are deliberately declared open in this version (to allow flexibility) at the cost of full automatic validation of every entry. A CDA R2 representation (HL7 CDA IPS IG) exists as an alternative encoding, and IHE's sIPS profile supplies document-sharing exchange guidance. Jurisdictions profile on top (e.g., the European Patient Summary and NRCeS INPS). An alternative representation is provided as templated HL7 CDA R2.
technical_features.inputs: The IPS consumes a patient's existing structured clinical data drawn from one or more health records or EHRs: conditions, allergies/intolerances, medication statements/orders, immunizations, diagnostic results (lab/pathology/radiology), procedures, device use, pregnancy status, social-history observations, vital signs, advance directives, alerts/flags, and optionally patient-authored narrative (Patient Story). It assumes codable source data; it does not itself ingest free dialogue or scanned images, and it defines no mechanism to extract a summary from unstructured text.
technical_features.outputs: A computable FHIR R4 IPS document: a Bundle.type=document whose first entry is the IPS Composition, with per-section entries pointing at the IPS-profiled resources listed above, validated against the IPS profiles. It can also be produced/consumed via the IPS $summary operation (a CapabilityStatement defines an IPS server's summarization capability). The content is intentionally exchange-oriented (cross-border/unplanned care) and is not a full medical record.
technical_features.standards_compliance: IPS is itself the standard and its conformance is formal: published, versioned FHIR R4 StructureDefinitions with bindings and constraints, an IG QA report, and dependency pinning (FHIR Extensions Pack 5.3.0, HL7 Terminology THO). It is the FHIR implementation of ISO 27269 (International patient summary), derived from CEN/EN 17269, and aligns with the European EHR Exchange Format (EEHRxF) and MyHealth@EU. Terminology: it uses SNOMED CT (including the freely usable Global Patient Set / SNOMED IPS Terminology), LOINC, RxNorm, UCUM, EDQM, and FHIR/HL7 code systems; bindings are mostly required only where globally agreed, otherwise preferred/extensible because freely usable global vocabularies (especially for medications) are incomplete. It is FHIR R4-based and R4B-compatible; the guide is Trial Use (STU 2) with intent to ballot normative later. It does not claim to validate fully automatically (slicing is open).
technical_features.offline_capability: The standard defines no offline mechanism - it is an exchange format. Offline behaviour is the implementer's problem, and IPS documents are self-contained Bundles, so a conformant IPS can be generated and stored locally and transmitted later. For MediKiosk this means IPS/INPS conformance is orthogonal to the offline constraint: the kiosk must supply its own local generation, storage, encryption and store-and-forward, while the document format itself travels cleanly.
technical_features.languages_supported: The IPS IG is authored in English and imposes no bilingual requirement; FHIR's language element and coded/translatable display fields allow localisation, and the base FHIR supports narrative in other languages. Real-world multi-language use is handled at the deployment layer: the European Patient Summary implementation translates the EU Patient Summary into supported languages, and IHE's sIPS supplies sharing guidance. There is no explicit Hindi/Devanagari/Hinglish provision in the IPS IG itself. [uncertain]
technical_features.deployment_model: Not applicable - IPS is a specification, not software. It runs wherever a conformant FHIR R4 server, client or summarizer runs; the IG provides a CapabilityStatement for IPS servers and a $summary operation. Jurisdictional deployments (e.g., MyHealth@EU National Contact Points in the EU, or NRCeS INPS within ABDM) implement it. No hardware requirement is stated.

performance_metrics.accuracy_or_quality_metrics: Not applicable in the model sense - IPS is a conformance specification with no accuracy/F1/ROUGE/BERTScore figures. Its measurable quality is conformance: an instance is valid if it validates against the IPS profiles (with the caveat that open slicing reduces how much can be checked automatically, a limitation the IG states explicitly).
performance_metrics.latency: Not applicable. No latency or time-to-summary figures exist for the specification; the $summary operation defines a capability, not a performance target.
performance_metrics.resource_requirements: Not applicable. As a data format, its footprint is the size of the summary document, which is deliberately minimal (three mandatory sections, more only as relevant). The resource cost falls entirely on whatever generates or consumes the bundle, not on the standard.
performance_metrics.scale_metrics: Adoption is broad but is measured in jurisdictions, not instances. As of 2025-2026, the EU cross-border programme MyHealth@EU has 10+ member states able to exchange European Patient Summary data (Estonia, Portugal, Croatia, Czech Republic, Malta, Spain, Luxembourg, Greece, Netherlands, France, Finland) with more in preparation, and 22 EU countries participating or planning; the EU has a legal mandate via the EHDS (patient summaries among the first priority data categories, exchange required from March 2029, implementing acts due March 2027). Internationally, 7+ countries have IPS development activity (Canada, New Zealand, NHS England, Haiti, Argentina, Netherlands, Cyprus), with G7-IPS and the Global Digital Health Partnership (GDHP) promoting it, and the Community of Interoperability Labs adopted IPS as the Asia eHealth Information Network core. India's NRCeS is building INPS on IPS. [uncertain] (these are approximate programme counts from a 2026 policy presentation, not an official HL7 adoption census).
performance_metrics.evaluation_protocol: Verification is by FHIR conformance testing: the IG publishes profiles, examples, a QA report, a CapabilityStatement and a $summary operation, and implementers validate instances with standard FHIR R4 validators/terminology servers. Cross-border implementations are additionally tested in EU connectathons/projectathons and via IHE sIPS. There is no clinical-outcome benchmark; the IG itself flags that full automatic validation is restricted by its open slicing rules.

milestone_significance.relevance_to_module_c: IPS is the single most important conceptual prior art for Module C: it proves that a standards body, not a vendor, has already defined the canonical shape of a 'patient summary document', and it does so as a screened, section-based Composition Bundle rather than a paragraph. Three things are directly load-bearing. First, the section taxonomy and its safety rule (mandatory Problems/Allergies/Medications; never omit a section silently - use emptyReason or an explicit 'no known X') is a ready-made, defensible structure for the kiosk's physician-facing summary, and it maps cleanly onto the clinical frameworks Module C already uses (SOCRATES/Dashavidha history plus structured meds/allergies/labs). Second, IPS's own known-issues list admits the two things MediKiosk cares most about are unsolved in the standard: representation of summarization activity (who summarized, what reconciliation was done - i.e., provenance) and method guidance for algorithmic vs human curation. That is precisely MediKiosk's stated per-field provenance plus physician-attestation differentiation, and IPS explicitly points to future work using the Provenance resource - so Module C can lead rather than merely conform. Third, and most concretely, NRCeS has now published the Indian Patient Summary (INPS) in the ABDM FHIR IG v7.0.0 preview, derived from IPS 2.0.0, with dual ABDM+IPS conformance and a dedicated 'Patient Story' section (plus Plan of Care, Social History) - giving Module C a plausible, standards-based structured home for a patient-elicited summary and materially changing the earlier open question that 'no NRCeS profile exists for patient-elicited summaries'.
milestone_significance.what_to_adopt_or_reject: Adopt: (1) the Composition-with-named-sections document model and the IPS section taxonomy as the skeleton of Module C's summary and as the reference for mapping to NRCeS INPS/OPConsultRecord; (2) the 'no silent omission' rule - every section either has entries or an explicit emptyReason/'no known X' statement, because it is a patient-safety property judges and clinicians will recognise; (3) the ISO 27269 minimalism discipline - a summary is a minimal, non-exhaustive, condition-independent extract, which fits the 2-5 minute OPD reality better than a full note dump; (4) the use of SNOMED CT (Global Patient Set), LOINC and UCUM for codes, and treatment of medications as MedicationStatement/Request; (5) the Patient Story concept as a natural slot for patient-elicited narrative, since it explicitly exists to carry 'what matters to the patient'. Reject or adapt: (1) do not treat IPS as the India output contract - MediKiosk must emit the NRCeS profile (INPS/OPConsultRecord), with IPS as the conceptual parent; (2) do not expect IPS to solve provenance or summarization attribution - the standard says it does not, so Module C must add per-field provenance and the physician attestation itself; (3) do not assume automatic validation - open slicing means conformance checking is partial, so the kiosk needs its own field-level checks; (4) do not assume IPS provides Hindi/bilingual output - localisation is a deployment concern the kiosk must own; (5) note the CDA encoding has minimal global uptake, so FHIR is the practical lane.
milestone_significance.limitations_and_risks: Several real limitations, several of them self-declared by HL7. (1) Provenance/summarization gap: IPS has no representation of who summarized, what reconciliation was performed, when/where, or whether content was algorithmically vs humanly curated - the exact area MediKiosk must supply itself. (2) Validation gap: all section slicing rules are open in STU 2, so the profile may technically allow inappropriate resources and cannot be fully automatically validated. (3) Vocabulary gap: globally recognised, freely usable vocabularies (especially for medication identification) are incomplete, so most bindings are preferred/extensible rather than required, weakening strict interoperability. (4) Maturity: it remains Trial Use (STU 2, maturity level 3), pending a future normative ballot, so details can change - and the 2.0.0 edition already carried breaking changes from 1.1.0. (5) No elicitation/offline/language story: IPS says nothing about extracting a summary from conversation or paper, nothing about offline operation, and nothing about India's languages - so it supplies a target shape, not a pipeline. (6) Licensing nuance: while the IG content is CC0, the code systems it references (SNOMED CT, LOINC, RxNorm) carry their own licences, which matters for a commercial kiosk. (7) Dependency churn: it depends on moving packages (FHIR Extensions, THO), and HL7 notes future alignment with the newer FHIR Clinical Documents IG is pending.
milestone_significance.differentiator_vs_medikiosk: IPS is a standard and a conceptual parent, not a competitor, and on balance it strengthens MediKiosk by validating the goal while leaving the hard parts open. IPS proves a standards-based summary document is legitimate and expected - which raises the bar (a kiosk without a standards-shaped summary looks behind), but it also means MediKiosk does not have to invent the document shape. Its declared gaps are exactly MediKiosk's claimed differentiators: IPS has no summarization provenance, no algorithmic-vs-human curation guidance, no offline model, no Hindi/bilingual output and no ABDM emission - whereas MediKiosk promises per-field provenance, elicit-never-diagnose, physician attestation, offline-first operation and NRCeS-conformant bilingual emission. The arrival of NRCeS INPS means the 'we define the patient summary' framing is gone, so MediKiosk's defensible edge is the patient-elicited structured history, the offline India-resident pipeline, the provenance/attestation layer and the AYUSH-aware clinical content - not the existence of a summary format.

business_info.license: The IPS Implementation Guide content is published under a CC0 notice (the IG footer carries the CC0 mark, consistent with HL7 FHIR IG licensing, and the related European PS IG states 'Copyright HL7 Europe. Licensed under creative commons public domain (CC0 1.0)'). The standard is freely usable and implementable. Important caveat: referenced code systems are separately licensed - SNOMED CT (though the freely usable Global Patient Set / SNOMED IPS Terminology is provided to support IPS without a full affiliate licence), LOINC, RxNorm, UCUM, EDQM - and implementers must respect those.
business_info.pricing: No cost to use the specification. There is no fee for the IG; costs, if any, arise from terminology licensing and implementation. HL7 membership is not required to implement (though it is needed to ballot).
business_info.funding: Developed and maintained by HL7 International in collaboration with CEN TC 251, ISO, SNOMED International and IHE, with public-sector and programme support (e.g., EU projects Xt-EHR/xShare/XpanDH and national programmes). No venture funding - it is SDO/programme funded.
business_info.commercial_status: A non-commercial international standards-development output (free standard), adopted by government programmes and vendors rather than sold. In the EU it is effectively on a regulatory path via the EHDS (patient summaries among the first priority data categories, exchanges required from March 2029 and implementing acts due by March 2027).

competition_ecosystem.competitors: Not a product market, but competing summary/record artifacts and exchange approaches: the ABDM NRCeS profiles (OPConsultRecord, HealthDocumentRecord, DischargeSummaryRecord) and the new INPS; the European Patient Summary IG (HL7 Europe, based on IPS); national/local patient-summary guides; and adjacent standards such as openEHR and IHE profiles. On the product side, ambient-scribe and intake vendors that emit structured notes (Abridge, Nuance DAX, Ambience, Eka Care/EkaScribe, Augnito) are the functional competitors for the 'who produces the summary' role - though they generate during/post-visit physician notes rather than a pre-visit patient-elicited IPS-shaped summary.
competition_ecosystem.integrations: IPS integrates at the exchange layer: HL7 FHIR R4/R4B and the FHIR $summary operation; IHE sIPS for document sharing; MyHealth@EU/eHDSI National Contact Points for cross-border exchange; the European EHR Exchange Format (EEHRxF)/EHDS; and jurisdictional profiling such as NRCeS INPS within ABDM (HIP/HIU, Health Locker). Terminology integrations are SNOMED CT (Global Patient Set/IPS Terminology), LOINC, RxNorm, UCUM and EDQM. Implementations commonly use FHIR tooling such as HAPI FHIR and the FHIR validator.
competition_ecosystem.ecosystem_notes: The ecosystem tailwind is regulatory. The EHDS Regulation entered into force in March 2025 and legally mandates patient-summary exchange (first priority data category) with implementing acts due by March 2027 and exchange obligations from March 2029; the European Patient Summary IG (ballot opened June 2026, supported by Xt-EHR) is being built on IPS to serve as the European basis. The G7-IPS roadmap, the Global Digital Health Partnership and the Asia eHealth Information Network core adoption all push IPS as the common summary. For India specifically, NRCeS folding INPS (based on IPS 2.0.0) into the ABDM IG v7.0.0 preview is the decisive signal: a MediKiosk that emits INPS-shaped output aligns simultaneously with ABDM and with the international IPS family, which is a strong judge-facing story - provided the emitted instance is validated against the NRCeS package, not merely 'IPS-like'.

history.release_date: The IPS concept originated in the 2010 EU/US eHealth Memorandum of Understanding (Trillium Bridge and the ONC S&I EHR work), with the first HL7 project (INTERPAS) promoted in April 2014. The FHIR IG's first public edition was STU 1 (v1.0.0, May 2020); the dataset was standardised as CEN/EN 17269:2019 and then ISO 27269 (2021). The CDA IG was published as STU in October 2018. [uncertain] (the exact first publication date of STU 1 FHIR v1.0.0 is given as 2020-05 in the version search dropdown).
history.key_milestones: 2010: EU/US eHealth MoU establishes the cross-Atlantic patient-summary effort (Trillium Bridge, ONC S&I). 2014-04: INTERPAS project promoted within HL7. 2016-05: European Commission grants CEN TC 251 engagement; CEN/HL7 agreement signed 2017. 2018-04 to 2019-08: FHIR STU 1 ballots v0.1.0 -> v0.3.0. 2018-10: HL7 CDA IPS IG published as STU. 2019: CEN/EN 17269:2019 published; SNOMED International launches the free Global Patient Set. 2020-05: FHIR IPS v1.0.0 (STU 1). 2020: myHealth@EU begins implementing eHN patient-summary guidelines; CEN/TS 17288 guidance. 2021: ISO 27269 replaces EN 17269. 2022-11: STU 1.1.0 unballoted update. 2022-10: COIL adopts IPS as the Asia eHealth Information Network core. 2024-08: STU 2.0.0-ballot. 2025-03: EHDS Regulation enters into force. 2025-10: STU 2.0.0 final (Edition 2, breaking changes from 1.1.0). 2026-06-17: HL7 Europe opens the European Patient Summary 1.0.0-ballot. 2026-06-18/19: IPS Edition 2.0.1 errata published.
history.recent_changes_last_6_months: The IPS moved twice in the six-month window and both matter to this sweep. On 2026-06-18 HL7 announced the errata publication of Edition 2.0.1 (specification generated 2026-06-19), an errata release after 2.0.0 that makes only non-substantive/corrective changes: it updates the dependency to FHIR Extensions Pack 5.3.0 (FHIR-57511), fixes incorrect FSH aliases for SNOMED CT/RxNorm/LOINC and adds an NDC alias (FHIR-57528), fixes incorrect LOINC and v3 display names and replaces inactive DICOM codes with LOINC (FHIR-57617), and updates SNOMED CT 'Structuring Terminology Choices' text (FHIR-57618). On 2026-06-17 HL7 Europe opened the ballot for the European Patient Summary IG 1.0.0-ballot (comments/votes through 31 August 2026), explicitly built on HL7 International's IPS and aligned to the EHDS/MyHealth@EU. In the same window, and most relevant to MediKiosk, NRCeS published the Indian Patient Summary (INPS) inside the ABDM FHIR IG v7.0.0 preview (generated 2026-07-15), derived from IPS version 2.0.0 and made dual-conformant to ABDM base profiles via the structuredefinition-imposeProfile extension - the first India-specific IPS derivative. No breaking normative change occurred in the window; the direction is consolidation and jurisdictional adoption.

market_positioning.target_users: National and regional health programmes and their vendors, EHR/PHR system makers, health-information-exchange operators, clinicians and patients - anyone who needs a portable, standards-based summary for unplanned or cross-border care. For MediKiosk, the relevant users are the standard-owning bodies (HL7), jurisdictional profilers (NRCeS/ABDM, HL7 Europe) and any implementer emitting or consuming a patient summary.
market_positioning.market_segment: Health-information interoperability standards - specifically patient-summary documents and cross-border/cross-system exchange. It sits alongside ABDM's clinical-artifact profiles and is the parent standard for India's INPS; it is not an intake, scribing or diagnostics product.
market_positioning.positioning_statement: In HL7's own words: 'An International Patient Summary (IPS) document is an electronic health record extract containing essential healthcare information about a subject of care. As specified in ISO 27269, it is designed for supporting the use case scenario for unplanned, cross border care, but it is not limited to it. It is intended to be international... The IPS dataset is minimal and non-exhaustive; specialty-agnostic and condition-independent; but still clinically relevant.'
